narrative_purpose: Visualizes the chapter's thought-experiment discipline: change one premise, then let ordinary consequences propagate outward instead of granting additional miracles.
subject: A long tabletop mechanism made from a row of ordinary wooden levers, brass pendulums, water cups and stone counterweights. At the far left, exactly one impossible element appears: a small rough stone floating unsupported a hand's breadth above the table, glowing faintly. The floating stone presses the first ordinary lever beneath it; that lever tips a cup, the water turns a small wheel, the wheel releases a counterweight, and the final counterweight lifts a wooden latch. Every stage after the single floating stone uses visible contact, weight, flowing water or gravity.
scene: A dark field-naturalist workshop, the mechanism stretching across a worn bench and fading into shadow, with no people present.
camera: Low oblique side view along the full length of the mechanism so each physical consequence can be followed from left to right.
light: The one floating stone supplies a cool living glow; the ordinary brass and water catch soft ambient highlights, with a restrained amber glint only on the final latch.
palette: Global cool dark workshop tones, teal glow isolated to the single impossible stone, scarce amber on brass contact points.
style: Painterly mechanical thought-experiment plate, tactile wood, stone, water and brass; observed rather than theatrical.
detail_level: Crisp on every contact point in the causal chain, softer workshop background and generous shadow around the mechanism.
composition: A clear left-to-right cascade beginning with one hovering stone and ending with one raised latch; no disconnected stages and ample dark space above for later callouts.
consistency_notes: There must be exactly one visually impossible element, the unsupported stone; every later motion must have an ordinary visible mechanical cause.
negative_prompt: no text, no arrows, no extra levitating objects, no perpetual-motion loop, no missing contact points, no steampunk clutter, no photographic or 3D-render look
